nameStory: The seaside pea gets its name from where it lives - right by the sea! Unlike garden peas that need rich soil and gentle care, this tough little plant thrives in the harsh conditions of coastal beaches. Its scientific name 'japonicus' means 'from Japan,' reflecting how this hardy species spans coastlines across the northern parts of the world.
description: Seaside pea is a sprawling beach plant that sends out trailing stems up to 3 feet long across sand and gravel. It's a member of the legume family, related to garden peas but built for coastal life. The plant stays low to the ground, spreading horizontally rather than climbing tall, with distinctive waxy blue-green leaves that help it survive salt spray and harsh sun.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, waxy blue-green leaves that feel almost rubbery to the touch, with 2-5 pairs of oval leaflets ending in a curly tendril instead of a final leaflet

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Broad pea-like flowers with deep purple 'banner' petals in back and lighter purple 'wing' petals on the sides, clustered in groups of up to twelve

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing trailing stems that sprawl horizontally across beaches rather than climbing upward, creating loose mats on sand and gravel

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Plump pea pods that rattle when shaken when mature, containing round seeds that can float in seawater

habitat: Look for seaside pea on sandy and gravelly beaches along New England's coast, especially on storm beaches where waves deposit debris. It thrives in the harsh transition zone between high tide and dune vegetation, often growing alongside beach grass and seaside goldenrod. You'll find it from Maine's rocky shores down to Connecticut's barrier beaches.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from thick underground stems, with the distinctive waxy blue-green leaves unfurling in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with showy purple pea flowers appearing from June through August, followed by developing seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and rattle in autumn winds, eventually splitting to release seeds that may wash away with winter storms.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, but the plant survives on thick underground rhizomes that can withstand winter storms and salt spray.

funFact: Seaside pea seeds can float in ocean water for months without losing their ability to sprout, which is how this plant managed to colonize beaches all around the northern Pacific and Atlantic oceans - it literally sailed the seas to spread around the world!
confusionNotes: Beach visitors sometimes mistake seaside pea for escaped garden sweet peas, but seaside pea's thick, waxy leaves and sprawling beach habitat are dead giveaways. Remember: if it's growing right on the beach and the leaves feel rubbery, it's the wild seaside pea, not a garden escape.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - while seaside pea is related to edible garden peas, coastal foragers should be cautious as some Lathyrus species can be toxic in large quantities. This plant is better appreciated for its ecological role in stabilizing beach sand than for its dinner table potential.
compareHints: Among New England's Lathyrus species, seaside pea is the only one with those distinctive thick, waxy blue-green leaves and strict beach habitat. Other sweet peas in the region have thinner, greener leaves and grow in meadows, marshes, or woodland edges rather than directly on ocean beaches. The coastal location and rubbery leaf texture make seaside pea unmistakable among its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's sweet peas, broad-leaved sweet pea stands out with its distinctly wide leaflets - most others like meadow pea have narrow, grass-like leaflets.
Among New England's wild peas, narrow-leaved everlasting-pea stands out with its bold pink flowers and strongly winged stems.
Among New England's wild peas, meadow pea stands out with its bright yellow flowers - most of its relatives like seaside pea and marsh pea have purple or pink blooms.
Among its Lathyrus relatives, marsh pea is distinguished by its wetland habitat and pinkish-purple flowers.

Unlike the broad-leaved sweet pea which has wider leaflets and no tubers, or the seaside pea which has 6-12 leaflets, tuberous pea is distinguished by its simple two-leaflet arrangement and underground tuber system.
Unlike its Lathyrus relatives in New England, spring vetch lacks the climbing tendrils found on species like broad-leaved sweet pea and narrow-leaved everlasting-pea.
Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, sweet pea stands out for its incredible fragrance and annual growth habit.

Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, pale vetchling stands out for its uniquely subdued flower color – while seaside pea has purple flowers, meadow pea is bright yellow, and broad-leaved sweet pea shows off in magenta.
Grass pea stands out from its New England Lathyrus cousins primarily by its unique brick-red flowers - no other sweet pea or vetchling in our region shares this color.
